passages.original: Partas namque ipsius quæ sunt nomina, secundum placitum sunt,et sine tempore.Nu]la namque in eane imaginatio quidem temporis:invenitur,sed habethoc quod partesejusextra significant.Totanamqueoratioest,Socrates cum Platone aliisque discipulis ; sed ejus pars Socrates, si a tota oratione disjuncta sit, significat aliquid. Nominis autem pars nihil extra significat; ipsius enim nominis quod est Socrates, quod disjunctum a tota connexione significat, partes nihil extra designant.Neque enim So,nequecra,neque tes,aliquid praeter totum nomen extra designant. Quare rectis-. sime diffinitio constituta est: Nomen essevocemsecundum placitum designativam sine tempore,cujus partes nihil extra significant.
passages.english: For its parts, which are names, are by convention and without time. For in it there is not even any image of time to be found, but it has this feature, that its parts signify something outside [the whole]. For the whole is a phrase: "Socrates with Plato and the other disciples"; but its part "Socrates", if it is separated from the whole phrase, signifies something. But the part of a name signifies nothing outside; for the parts of the name itself, "Socrates", which signifies [something] when separated from the whole combination, designate nothing outside. For neither "So" nor "cra" nor "tes" designates anything outside, apart from the whole name. Therefore the definition has been set down most correctly: a name is a vocal sound that signifies by convention, without time, whose parts signify nothing outside.
passages.notes: Several words run together or misread in the scan (e.g. "Partas" for "Partes", "Nu]la", "eane"); translated as the evident readings.

passages.original: Ratio autem ejus in aliis quidem eadem est,sed cliffert.Quoniam cum est, vet fuit,erit, adjunctum, neque verum neque falsum est ; nomen vero semper, ut Catonis est, vel non est, nondum enim aliquid verum dicit aut falsum.
passages.english: Its account, however, is in other respects the same, but it differs. For when "is", or "was", or "will be" is added, [the result] is either true or false; but the name always, as "of Cato" [is], or is not [is not so]; for it does not yet say anything true or false.
passages.notes: The passage is garbled. "cliffert" is read as "differt" and "vet" as "vel". As printed, the text says that with "is/was/will be" added it is "neither true nor false", which contradicts the argument. The sense required is that the oblique case ("of Cato") with "is" added is neither true nor false, while the nominative becomes true or false. The clause "nomen vero semper, ut Catonis est, vel non est" is obscure, and the translation follows the words only loosely.

passages.original: Ergo eadem diffinitio ratioque nominis est et casus nomiuis, sed his una additur differentia, quod omne nomen cum eo quod diciturest,autnon est conjunctum,aut affirmativam enuntiationem facit,aut negativam,ut Socrates est, vel Socrates non est.Hic enim quonam ventas aut falsitas incidit, enuntiationem esse necesse est ; in casibus vero quamvis addas est, aut non est, nulla inde affirmatio neque negatio fit.Neque enim in hos ulla veritas aut falsitas cadit.
passages.english: Therefore the definition and account of a name and of a case of a name are the same, but to these one differentia is added: that every name, when joined with "is" or "is not", makes either an affirmative or a negative statement, as "Socrates is" or "Socrates is not". For here, since truth or falsity occurs, it must be a statement; but in the cases, although you add "is" or "is not", no affirmation or negation results from it. For no truth or falsity falls upon these.

passages.original: Haec enim differentia quae est non currit, et non laborat,quae a verbo puro et simplici distat, nullo apud antiquiores vocabulo nuncupata est. Differentiam autem vocavit id quod dicitur non currit, et non Jaborat, ab eo quod est currit et Iaborat.Sed quoniam his nullum estnomenab antiquisimpositum,Aristoteles nomen ipse constituit dicens:Sit verbum infinitum.Alioqui maximam rJubitationem facit hujus praedicamenti similitudo, quod ipsumquidempraedicamentumvox est designativa secundum placitum ,el de altero praedicatur, et consignificat tempus, idem scilicet quod verbum quod est currit.
passages.english: For this difference, which is "does not run" and "does not labour", and which stands apart from the pure and simple verb, was called by no name among the older writers. He called a "difference" what is said, "does not run" and "does not labour", as against "runs" and "labours". But since no name had been imposed on these by the ancients, Aristotle himself established a name, saying: "Let it be an indefinite verb." Otherwise the likeness of this predicate causes very great doubt, because this predicate is itself a sound significant by convention, is predicated of something else, and co-signifies time, that is, the same as the verb "runs".
passages.notes: Scanning errors read as Jaborat/Iaborat = laborat and rJubitationem = dubitationem.

passages.original: Naturalium vero su pellectiles sunt naturales, ut oculi instrumenta quidem sunt videndi,qui visus res naturalis est. Quare oculos quoque naturales esse necesse est,ita etiam oratorio rerum naturalium su- pellexest,atque instrumentum,id est sententiarum. Quare ipsa quoque oratio est naturalis.Aristoteles autem dicit, non secundum naturam esse orationem,sed secundum placitum. Quocirca nec orationem esse suppellectilem naturalem. Quod enim dicit, non sicut instrumentum,non dicit non perhoc instrumentum sensa proferri,sed tantum rem esse orationem secundum positionem,per quas proprias sententias demonstremus.
passages.english: Now the implements of natural things are natural; for instance, the eyes are instruments of seeing, and sight is a natural thing. Therefore the eyes too must be natural. So too speech is an implement and instrument of natural things, that is, of thoughts. Therefore speech itself is also natural. Aristotle, however, says that speech is not according to nature but according to convention. Therefore speech is not a natural implement either. For when he says "not as an instrument", he does not say that thoughts are not expressed through this instrument, but only that speech is a thing [existing] by imposition, through which we may show our own thoughts.

passages.original: Totum vero quod dicit tale est:en untiativæ orationes si sunt simplices,has verba constituunt. Ex duobus enim nominibus solis enunLiatio non fit,ex nomine autem et verbo iit, ut est, homo vivit.Fit quoque ex solis verbis ut est,arnbulare moveri est.Fit etiam exca- su verbi, ut Socrates fuit, vel etiam,dies erit. Erit enim et fuit verbicasussunt.Quocircaenuntiativam orationem simplicem sola maxime verba constituunt.Eorumque ponit exemplum ,in quo cumplura sint nomina, nisi addito tamen verbo in enuntiationis proprietatem et significantiam non venit, utest definitio hominis.(Ratio enim hominis est speciei deti- nitio.y Cui si non aut est, aut non est,aul aliquid hujusmodi addatur,enuntiatio esse non poterit.Nam si quis dicat, Animal rationale mortale,nulla in eo adhuc falsitas autveritas intelligitur.
passages.english: The whole of what he says is this: statement-making phrases, if they are simple, are constituted by verbs. For a statement does not come about from two names alone, but it does from a name and a verb, as "a man lives". It comes about also from verbs alone, as "to walk is to be moved". It comes about also from a case of a verb, as "Socrates was", or also "it will be day". For "will be" and "was" are cases of the verb. Therefore verbs above all, alone, constitute a simple statement-making phrase. And he gives an example of them, in which, although there are several names, nevertheless unless a verb is added it does not attain the character and signification of a statement, such as the definition of man. (For the account of man is the definition of the species.) If to this neither "is" nor "is not" nor anything of this sort is added, it cannot be a statement. For if someone says "rational mortal animal", no falsity or truth is yet understood in it.

passages.original: Idcirco enim verba et nomine dictiones solum Bunt, quoniam cum dicta fuerint simplicia, sive aliquo proferente, id est sponte - cente, sive ad alterius interrogationem aliquo respondente,neque verum ex his neque falsum valet intelligi. Si quis enim per se dicat : Socrates, vel rursus per se solum simplexque, ambulat, neque verum efficit, neque falsum. Si vero alio interrogante,Socratesne ambulat? ille reepondeat,Ambulat,si huic ipsi verbo per se quisquam velit adver- tere quod dixit ambulat, enuntiatio nulla eat,quod et cum superiore interrogatione conjungat,tunc ex interrogationisetresponsionis conjunctione nascitur enuntiatio.Solum autem nomen vel verbum neque dicente aliquo, et sponte proferente, nec respondente, potest quisquam dicere, quoniam enuntiatio facta est.
passages.english: For verbs and names are only expressions for this reason: because when they are said on their own, whether someone utters them, that is, says them of his own accord, or someone answers to another's question, neither truth nor falsity can be understood from them. For if someone says by itself "Socrates", or again, by itself alone and simple, "walks", he produces neither truth nor falsity. But if, when another asks, "Does Socrates walk?", he answers "Walks", if anyone wishes to attend to this very verb by itself, that he said "walks", there is no statement; but if he joins it with the preceding question, then a statement arises from the conjunction of question and answer. But of a name or verb alone, whether someone says it and utters it of his own accord or answers, no one can say that a statement has been made.
passages.notes: "sponte - cente" read as "sponte dicente"; "quod et cum" apparently for "quod si cum" ("but if he joins").

passages.original: Nunc quid oratio sitsimplex compositaque declarat. Est enim simplex oratio quæ duobus terminis constat. Tertimi autem sunt nomina et verba, quae in simplici propositione prædicamus,ut in eo quod est, Socrates disputat,Socrates et disputat termini sunt.et qui minor terminus in enuntiatione proponitur ,ut Socrates,subjectus dicitur,et ponitur prior; qui vero major, prædicatur,et locatur posterior,ut disputat.
passages.english: Now he explains what a simple and a composite phrase is. A simple phrase is one which consists of two terms. The terms are the names and verbs which we predicate in a simple proposition; as in "Socrates debates", "Socrates" and "debates" are the terms. And the lesser term that is put forward in the statement, such as "Socrates", is called the subject and is placed first; but the greater is predicated and is placed after, such as "debates".

passages.original: Hoc autem pertinet ad affirmationem,ut aliquid de aliquo prædices. Ad negationem vero, ut unum aliquid ab uno aliquo praedicando disjungas, ut in eo quod est, ;Socrates non disputat, disputare unum terminum,a non Socrate alio termino,prædicando disjunxi.Aliæ vero suntoratione;; enuntiativae, quae compositæ nominantur ,quæ ex simplicibus orationibus componuntur, ut est, sesest,lux es;
passages.english: This belongs to affirmation: that you predicate something of something. But to negation: that by predicating you separate some one thing from some one thing; as in "Socrates does not debate", I have, by predicating, separated one term, "to debate", from the other term, "Socrates". But there are other statement-making phrases which are called composite, which are composed from simple phrases, as is "[if it] is [day], it is light";
passages.notes: The example is garbled ("sesest,lux es"); from the following context it should be "si dies est, lux est" ("if it is day, it is light"). "a non Socrate" read as "a Socrate".

passages.original: Postquam de compositis orationibus simplicibus- quetractavit,diffioitionem en untiationis per affirmationem et negationem ingreditur;ait enim:Enuntiatio est vox signidcans affirmationem vel negationem, vel in præteritum,vel in præsens, vel in futurum tempus.Quod enim dixit,de eo quod esl,ad affirmationem retulit; quod addit,vel non est,ad negationem; quod vero secutus est,quemadmodum tempora divisa sunt,ad singulorum,temporum retuMtrationem; sive enim aliquis dicat: Socrates vivit,Socrates non vivit,sive Socrates vixil,Socrates non vixil,vel sic : Socrates victurus est,Socrates victurus non est,quoniam affirmatio est aut negatio,et quoniam quaelibet ipsarum in aliquo temporum est,quæ dividuntur in futurum, praesens ac præteritum, plenam retinet simplicis enuntiationis naturam.
passages.english: After he has treated composite and simple phrases, he proceeds to the definition of the statement by way of affirmation and negation; for he says: a statement is a vocal sound signifying affirmation or negation, in past, present, or future time. What he said, "concerning what is", he referred to affirmation; what he adds, "or is not", to negation; and what he went on to, "as the times are divided", he referred to the account of each of the times. For whether someone says "Socrates lives", "Socrates does not live", or "Socrates lived", "Socrates did not live", or thus: "Socrates will live", "Socrates will not live", since it is an affirmation or negation, and since each of them is in one of the times, which are divided into future, present and past, it retains the full nature of a simple statement.

passages.original: Universale est quod de pluribus prædicatur,ut homo de pluribus dicitur, et est uni- veraalia. Singulare vero est, ut quaelibet res iodivi. dua, cujus nulla praedicatio ad sibimet subjecta per- veniat, ut Plato vel Socrates; horum autem naturam docet exemplis, ait enim: Ut bomo quidem un iver- sale, Plato vero eorum quæ sunt singularia. Nam si hoc est universale quod de pluribus prædicatur, ho- mo universale est, de pluribus enim individuis dicitur.
passages.english: A universal is what is predicated of many, as "man" is said of many, and is among universals. A singular is, for instance, any individual thing whose predication does not reach any [things] subject to it, such as Plato or Socrates. He teaches their nature by examples, for he says: "As man is a universal, and Plato is among the singulars." For if a universal is what is predicated of many, man is a universal, since it is said of many individuals.

passages.original: Atque hoc est quod ait, Necesse est autem enuntiare quod inest aIiquid,aut non,aliquoties quidem eorum alicui quae sunt universalia. Homo enim cum sit universale animal illi inesse affirmatio proposuit. Quae dixit, Homo animal est, et non inesse negatio quae ait, Homo animal non est. Si vero aliquis SiD dicat: Socrates disputat, Socrates non disputat, alicui eorum quae sunt singularia esse et non esse conjunxit. Et boc est quodait: AHquotiesautem eorum quae sunt singularia. Nam cum Socrates singulare quiddam sit,disputatio ei ab affirmationejun- cta est, sed a negatione sejuncta.
passages.english: And this is what he says: "It is necessary to state that something belongs or does not, sometimes to one of the things that are universal." For since man is universal, the affirmation which said "Man is an animal" proposed that animal belongs to him, and the negation which says "Man is not an animal" that it does not belong. But if someone says "Socrates debates", "Socrates does not debate", he has joined being and not being to one of the things that are singular. And this is what he says: "But sometimes [to one] of the things that are singular." For since Socrates is something singular, debating is joined to him by the affirmation, but separated by the negation.
passages.notes: "SiD" is a stray scanning error, omitted.

passages.original: Quæcunque igitur contradictiones universalium sum universaliter,necesse est alteram esse veram vel jalsam.Et quæcunque in singularibus sunt,ut Socrates albus est,non est Socrates albus.
passages.english: Therefore, whatever contradictions of universals are [stated] universally, it is necessary that one be true or false. And whatever are in singulars, as "Socrates is white", "Socrates is not white".
passages.notes: "alteram esse veram vel falsam" is presumably for "alteram veram, alteram falsam" (one true, the other false); translated as it stands.

passages.original: Dico autem, ut est Socrates albus, non est Socrates albus.
passages.english: I mean, as "Socrates is white", "Socrates is not white".

passages.original: Sensus huj usmodi est,si autem aliud aliquid prædicaverit negatio quam affirmatio prædicavit, vel si de alio subjecto idem negatio prædicaverit quod in affirmatione fuerit prædicatum, non sunt sibi oppositae, sed a se tantum diversæ sunt.si quis enim dicat, Socrates disputat, et aliud respondeat, Socrates non ambulat, diversum prædicatum est, etdiversæ sunt propositiones, et non oppositæ,et hoc est quod dixit.Si autem aliud aliquid, aliud enim praedicavit negatio quam affirmatio praedicaverat .Quod si quis sic dicat, Socrales disputat, aliusque respondeat, Plato non disputat,dealio subjecto idem prædicavit, . et sunt a se diversae propositiones,et non oppositæ. Eterit id quod ait aliquis, vel de alio idem. Quod si utraque sint diversa, multo magis propositiones diversae fiunt, quibus positis ad proposita rursus exempla conlendit, et uni aFfirmationi uuam enuntiationem negationis opponit,angularibus angulares, af'firmativis negativas, particularibus universales, indefinitis indefinitas opponens et comparans.
passages.english: The sense is of this kind: but if the negation predicates something other than what the affirmation predicated, or if the negation predicates of another subject the same thing that was predicated in the affirmation, they are not opposed to each other, but are merely different from each other. For if someone says, "Socrates is disputing," and another replies, "Socrates is not walking," the predicate is different, and the propositions are different and not opposed; and this is what he said: "But if something else," for the negation predicated something other than the affirmation had predicated. But if someone speaks thus, "Socrates is disputing," and another replies, "Plato is not disputing," he has predicated the same thing of another subject, and the propositions are different from each other and not opposed. And this will be what he says, "or the same of another." But if both are different, the propositions become all the more different. Having set these out, he turns again to the examples proposed, and opposes one enunciation of negation to one affirmation, opposing and comparing singulars to singulars, negatives to affirmatives, universals to particulars, indefinites to indefinites.

passages.original: Cum enim id quod factum est dicitur factum, definite verum est, quod si id factum esse denegetur, falsum est definite; siveergo in universalibus universaliter prædicatis contradictio per oppositionem particularitatis fiat, sive in singularibus, ut in Socrate et in cæteris individuis in his quoque quæ sunt præterita, semper una vera est, altera falsa, ut in eo quod est, Socrates veneno peremptus est. Socrates veneno peremptus non est, vera est affirmatio definite, et ita rursus falsa negatio est in præsentibus quoque idem esse necesse est.
passages.english: For when what has been done is said to have been done, it is definitely true; but if it is denied that it has been done, it is definitely false. So whether the contradiction is made in universals predicated universally by the opposition of particularity, or in singulars, as with Socrates and other individuals, in these also which are past one is always true, the other false: as in "Socrates was killed by poison," "Socrates was not killed by poison," the affirmation is definitely true, and so again the negation is false. In present things too the same must hold.

passages.original: In singularibus vero, et (uturis non similiter.- Propositionum aliæ sunt tantum inesse significantes, ut si quis Socrate vivo dixisset : Socrates calvus est, alius negaret, Socrates calvus non est. Illa enim inesse posuit Socrati calvitiem, illa calvitiem a 80- crate disjunxit. Aliae vero sunt necessariæ, ut si quis dicat, Necesse est solem annis omnibus in Arietem rursus redire. Rem namque necessariam et ex necessitate evenientem prædicaus, totam fecit necessariam propositionem.
passages.english: "But in singulars and future things it is not similar." Of propositions, some signify only being-in (inherence), as if, while Socrates was alive, someone had said, "Socrates is bald," and another denied, "Socrates is not bald." For the one posited baldness as being in Socrates, the other separated baldness from Socrates. Others are necessary, as if someone says, "It is necessary that the sun returns again into Aries every year." For by predicating a thing that is necessary and comes about of necessity, he made the whole proposition necessary.

passages.original: Rursus cum negatio necessaria non sit, interdum accidit, ut affirmatio contingat. Quare hæc hujusmodi eveniendi et non eveniendi potentia, utrumlibet vocatur. Quod in his utrumlibet, id est vel atfirmationes vel negationes, evenire conceditur. Nunc ergo Aristoteles hoc validissima argumentatione contendit astruere, quod quemadmodum :n præteritis, et in his quæ sunt præsentia, non modoin affirmatione et negatione, unam veram, alteram falsam esse necesse est, sed definite una vera est, definite altera suscipit falsitatem, non ita in his quae contingentes vocantur.
passages.english: Again, since the negation is not necessary, it sometimes happens that the affirmation comes about. Therefore this kind of capacity for happening and not happening is called "either way" (*utrumlibet*), because in these things it is granted that either one may happen, that is, either the affirmations or the negations. Now, therefore, Aristotle seeks to establish by a very strong argument that in past things and in present things, in affirmation and negation, it is not only necessary that one be true and the other false, but that one is definitely true and the other definitely takes on falsity; whereas this is not so in those [things] that are called contingent.

passages.original: In his enim quae sunt futura vel contingentia, non esse affirmationes et negationes veras vel falsas definite probare contendit. Nam si unus dicat aliquid futurum, alius neget, ut utraque eveniant, fieri non potest ; quis enim dixerit, dicente aliquo Socrates cœ- naturus est, alioque negante Socrates crenaturus non est, utrasqueveras in uno eodemque contingere? Hoc igitur fieri non potest ; unus ergo eorum verum dicturus. est alius mentietur : ponatur enim una eorum definite vera esse, vel falsa, si ergo omnis affir- mafio et negatio vera vel falsa est definite, et uterque negans affirmansque veri in contradictionibus esse non possunt, necesse est unum verum dicere.
passages.english: For he strives to prove that in things which are future or contingent, affirmations and negations are not definitely true or false. For if one person says that something will be and another denies it, it cannot happen that both come about; for who would say, when someone says "Socrates is going to dine" and another denies "Socrates is not going to dine," that both occur true in one and the same [thing]? This therefore cannot happen; so one of them will speak truly, the other will lie. For let one of them be posited as definitely true or false: if therefore every affirmation and negation is definitely true or false, and both the denier and the affirmer cannot be in the truth in contradictions, it is necessary that one says the true,

passages.original: non igitur verum est omnem affirmationem vel negationem veram esse definite vel falsam.Omnia autem ex necessitatecontingere, si illæ detmite verae vel falsae sunt,talis syllogismus ostendit: omnisin futurum definita veritas vel falsitas eventum rei vel futurum vel non futurum ex necessitate conslituit, sed omnes propositiones futurae definite veræ vel falsae sunt.ln omnibus igitur eveniendi, vel non eve. niendi necessitas erit, pro qua conclusione illud Aristoteles intulit, quod ait :
passages.english: Therefore it is not true that every affirmation or negation is definitely true or false. And the following syllogism shows that all things come about from necessity if those [statements] are definitely true or false: every definite truth or falsity about the future establishes by necessity the outcome of a thing, either that it will be or that it will not be; but all future propositions are definitely true or false; therefore in all things there will be a necessity of happening or not happening. In place of this conclusion Aristotle brought in what he says:
passages.notes: The passage ends at a colon, before the quotation from Aristotle.

passages.original: Validam sibi ipsi vim argumentationis opponit,qua possit ostendere affirmationes negationesque veras vel falsas esse definite, et ait providendum esse ne forte necesse sit suspicari id quod jam factum est vere dici potuisse antequam fieret,esse faciendum, ut si Socrates hesterna nocte cænavit, verum fuit hesterna matutina dicere, quoniam coenaturus est; quocirca definite quoque verum fuisset, seeo pra'diceretur. Omnia igi).ur ea quae fiunt definite poterant vera prædicari.
passages.english: He sets against himself a strong force of argument by which it could be shown that affirmations and negations are definitely true or false, and says one must take care lest perhaps it be necessary to suppose that what has already happened could truly have been said, before it happened, to be going to happen: as, if Socrates dined last night, it was true yesterday morning to say that he is going to dine; therefore it would also have been definitely true, if it were predicted. So all things that happen could have been definitely predicated as true.

passages.original: Manifestum est quoniam etiam in singularibus, si est verum interrogatum negare,quod et alfirmare verum est, ut, Putasne Socrates sapiens est? Non, Socrates igitur non sapiens est. In unwersalibus vero non est vern quæ similiter dicilur. Vera est aulem nellatio, ut Putasne omnis hnmo sapiens est? Non. Omnis igitur horno non sapiens est, hoc enim est falsum ;
passages.english: "It is evident that also in singulars, if it is true to deny what is asked, it is also true to affirm, as: 'Do you think Socrates is wise?' 'No.' 'Therefore Socrates is not-wise.' But in universals what is said in a similar way is not true; rather the negation is true, as: 'Do you think every man is wise?' 'No.' 'Therefore every man is not-wise': for this is false;
passages.notes: Text heavily garbled by scanning ("vern", "nellatio", "hnmo"); read as "vera", "negatio", "homo".

passages.original: Quoties aliquis, inquit, in singularibus rebus interrogat,et is qui interrogalur,negat, tunc is qui interrogat recte negationem cum singularijungens, ex infinito nomine faciet affirmationem, ut si aliquis dicat: Putasne Socrates sapiens est ? contra alius respondeat, Non, erit recta conclusio dicentis: Socrates igitur non sapiens est.Ex negatione ergo re- spondentis et infinito nomine non sapiens, facta est affirmatio, Socrates non sapiens est, atque hoc quidem in singularibus.
passages.english: Whenever someone, he says, asks about singular things, and the one asked denies, then the questioner, rightly joining the negation with the singular, will make an affirmation from an indefinite name: as if someone says, "Do you think Socrates is wise?" and the other answers in reply, "No," the conclusion of the speaker will be correct: "Therefore Socrates is not-wise." So from the negation of the respondent and the indefinite name "not-wise," an affirmation has been made, "Socrates is not-wise"; and this indeed in singulars.

passages.original: Ordo autem sermonum talis est.Quoniam vera, inquit, quaedam sunt, quae ita conjuncta de aliquo prædicantur,ut eorum praedicamentum unum sit,et in unum congruat forma eorum quæ extra vere o- terant prædicari,ut in eo quod est animal bipes de homine juncta compositaque dicuntur, et fit una quodammodo prædicatio: cum animal et bipes extra sigillatim valeant prædicari, dicimus enim homo animal est,et rursus homo bipes est, alia vero quæ non sunt eo modo,quæ sigillatim quidem praedicari verum est,composita vero falsum, sed quae horum differentia est, vel quando illud,quando hoc eveniat, dicendum est, et hoc docet exemplis. De homine enim, in quit, verum est dicere extra anima!, extra bipes, et ut unum, ut de eo dicatur, animal bipes. Rursum quemlibet hominem, ut Socratem possumus dicere, ille homo albus est, rursus ille bomo homo est,et haec ut unum juncta dicentes: ille homo homo albus est. Sed aliquoties evenit ut aliquis homo citharcedus sitquidem et iwperitus.Bonusau- tem homo,et si de ipso dicatur quoniam est citbarædus,verum cst,et quia bonus est hoc quoque verum est.Sed non et si citharœdus estet bonus,idcirco jam bonus est etiam citharœdus,fortasse enim est impe- ritissimua, homo autem bonus.
passages.english: The order of the words is as follows. Since, he says, there are some true things which are predicated of something so joined that their predicate is one, and the form of those which could also truly be predicated separately comes together into one—as in "two-footed animal," which are said joined and compounded of man, and there comes to be in a way one predication, while "animal" and "two-footed" can be predicated separately, for we say "man is an animal" and again "man is two-footed"—while others are not of that kind, which it is true to predicate separately but false compounded, we must say what the difference between these is, or when the one, when the other, happens; and this he teaches by examples. For of a man, he says, it is true to say separately "animal," separately "two-footed," and as one, so that "two-footed animal" is said of him. Again, of any man, such as Socrates, we can say "that man is white," again "that man is a man," and, saying these joined as one, "that man is a white man." But it sometimes happens that some man is a cithara-player yet unskilled, but a good man; and if it is said of him that he is a cithara-player, it is true, and that he is good, this too is true. But it does not follow that, if he is a cithara-player and good, he is therefore also a good cithara-player; for perhaps he is most unskilled, but a good man.

passages.original: In his, in quit, quae prædicantur, et de his de qai- bus illa ipsa prædicantur, duplex ratio est.Aut enim duo accidentia de uno subjecto dicunlur,ut Marius malus est,Marius duxest; aut unum accidens de uno subjecto praedicantur, aliud vero accidens de illo praedicato accidenti prædicatur, ut si quis dicat : Cicero est calvus,calvus orator est.Hic enim calvus de subjecto Cicerone, orator de calvo pra'dicatur. Hoc est enim quod ait : Quaecunque secundum acci- densdicuntur, veeeodem, vel alterum de altero eeodem, usqua uoaccidentia euno prædicentur ;
passages.english: "In those things," he says, "which are predicated, and concerning those of which they are predicated, the account is twofold." For either two accidents are said of one subject, as "Marius is bad" and "Marius is a general"; or one accident is predicated of one subject and another accident is predicated of that predicated accident, as if someone says, "Cicero is bald, the bald [man] is an orator." For here "bald" is predicated of the subject Cicero, and "orator" of "bald". For this is what he says: "Whatever things are said accidentally, either of the same thing, or one of the other ... of the same, so that two accidents are predicated of one;"
passages.notes: The lemma is badly garbled ("veeeodem ... usqua uoaccidentia euno"). It is reconstructed as "vel de eodem, vel alterum de altero ... de eodem, ut duo accidentia de uno praedicentur".

passages.original: Dicit enim: Callias homo albus albus est,idcirco quoniam albus in homine albo continebatur, quod ante de CaIliaprædi- catum est. Atque hoc est quod ait : Quare neque album frequenter. Alia vero sunt quae hoc in prolatione non habent, sed in natura, si quis enim sic dicat : Socrates So::rates est, et rursus Socrates homo est, et haec simul Jungat, ut dicat Socrates Socrates homo est, non recte fecerit prædicationem. Nam homo in Socrate inerat, et rursus bomo de Socrate praedicatum est.
passages.english: For he says, "Callias is a white man white," because "white" was contained in "white man," which had previously been predicated of Callias. And this is what he says: "So that neither 'white' repeatedly." But there are others which have this not in the utterance but in the nature: for if someone speaks thus, "Socrates is Socrates," and again "Socrates is a man," and joins these together, so as to say "Socrates is Socrates man," he will not have made a correct predication. For "man" was in "Socrates," and again "man" has been predicated of Socrates.

passages.original: sed hoc non in omnibus eveniet.Nam si qua hujusmodi sit præ di- catio,in qua aliquid oppositum addatur ipsi prædicationi,præter illud oppositum,simpliciter illa prædicatio non potest prædicari,ut si quis dicat de Socrate jam mortuo, quoniam hoc quod jacet, bomo mortuus est,vere dicit,simpliciterautem dicere non potest, hoc quod jacet homo est. Idcirco quoniam additum est prædicato, id est homini, id quodho- mini oppositum est,id est mortuus.
passages.english: but this will not happen in all cases. For if there is a predication of such a kind that something opposed is added to the predication itself, then apart from that opposite the predication cannot be predicated simply: as if someone says of Socrates already dead that "this which lies here is a dead man," he speaks truly, but he cannot say simply "this which lies here is a man." This is because there has been added to the predicate, that is, to "man," what is opposed to "man," that is, "dead."

passages.original: Quando autem hujusmodi oppositioni ei quod prædicatur, non jungitur, potest simpliciter vere prædicari, sed nec hoc semper, magisque illud verius dicitur, quoniam cum ista oppositio est, nunquam verum est eorum qua: juncta vere prædicantur, simpliciter vere aliquid appellari. Cum autem ista oppositio non inest, noa semper vere simpliciter praedicari eorum aliquid, quas de aliquo vere juncta dicuntur. Si quis enim sic dicat : Homerus polea est, verum dixerit ; quod si dicat : Homerus est simpliciter praeter poetam, falsum est. Atqui esse et polea, non sunt opposita. Ergo nonsemper quando oppositio non est in prædicalis, verum est aliquid simpliciter prædicari.
passages.english: But when such an opposition is not joined to what is predicated, it can be predicated simply and truly; yet not even this always, and the following is said more truly: since, when that opposition is present, it is never true that any of the things truly predicated in combination is called truly in a simple way; but when that opposition is not present, it is not always [true that] any of the things truly said in combination of something is truly predicated simply. For if someone says, "Homer is a poet," he will have spoken truly; but if he says, "Homer is," simply, apart from "poet", it is false. Yet "to be" and "poet" are not opposites. Therefore it is not always true, when there is no opposition in the predicates, that something is predicated simply.
passages.notes: The second sentence is elliptical in the Latin.

passages.original: Quidam volentes id quod non est, aliquo modo esse monstrare, tali utebantursyljogismo, quod est opinabile est. Concludebant quod non est igitur est, docentes ea quæ essent, sca potus, non opinabilia esse; quo autem non es, opinioni aum subjacere, nulla etiam scientia claudio Quod Aristoteles hoc modo discutit : ait enim, non idcirco est opinabile, quoniam est, sed idcirco opinabile est, quoniam non est; sed hoc quod non est, est quidem aliquid, sed est non per se, sed opinabile. Et quemadmodum Homerus quidem est quiddam, id est poeta, non tamen est per se, ita id quod non eSI, est quidem aliquid, id est opinabile, vel ignorabile, vel nescibile, non tamen est aliquid per se in natura.
passages.english: Certain people, wishing to show that what is not in some way is, used this syllogism: what is not is an object of opinion. They concluded: therefore what is not is. They taught that things which are are, rather, not objects of opinion, while what is not is subject to opinion and is enclosed by no knowledge. Aristotle refutes this in this way. For he says that it is not an object of opinion because it is, but it is an object of opinion because it is not. And what is not is indeed something, but it is not [so] in itself; [it is] an object of opinion. And just as Homer is something, that is, a poet, yet is not in himself, so what is not is indeed something, that is, an object of opinion, or unknown, or unknowable, yet it is not something in itself in nature.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors are corrected by sense: "sca potus" is read as "scientiae potius" (?), "aum" as "eum", and "claudio" as "claudi". The phrase "ea quae essent ... non opinabilia esse" is uncertain.

passages.original: ad se invicem, hæ scilicet quæ sunt de possibili esse et non possibili, de conlingenti et non contingenti, de imp os- sibili et necessario. lIabent enim aliquas dubitationes. Propositionum alix sunt quae simpliciter profcruo- tur, aliae quibus aliquis modus in enuntiatione mi- scelur. Si quis enim dicat : Socrates disputat, simplicem propositionem fccit; si vero aliquis dicat: Socrates bene disputat, modum propositioni quam enuntiabat adjunxit; quomodo enim disputaret ap-' posuit, cum dixit bene. Nunc ergo boc speculatur quemadmodum se habent affirmationr.s et negaLioDes earum propositionum, quae cum modo aliquo profe- runlur, ut siquis dicat, possibile est boc fieri, et rur- sua, non possibile est hoc fieri, quemadmodum sese in his affirmationis habeat negationisque natura.
passages.english: to one another, namely those which concern being possible and not possible, being contingent and not contingent, being impossible and necessary. For they involve certain difficulties. Of propositions, some are uttered simply, while others have some mode mixed into the statement. For if someone says, "Socrates is debating," he has made a simple proposition; but if someone says, "Socrates is debating well," he has added a mode to the proposition he was stating; for when he said "well," he added how he was debating. So now [Aristotle] examines how the affirmations and negations of those propositions stand which are uttered with some mode, as if someone should say, "it is possible for this to happen," and again, "it is not possible for this to happen": how the nature of affirmation and negation stands in these.
passages.notes: The passage opens mid-sentence, continuing the lemma in the text before the passage ("how affirmations and negations are related"). Several scanning errors were silently corrected (e.g. "conlingenti" for contingenti, "imp os- sibili" for impossibili, "profcruo- tur" for proferuntur, "boc" for hoc).

passages.original: Conversae autem se sequuntur, quoniam affirmatio non sequitur affirmationem, et negatio negationem, sed affirmationem negationes, ne- gationefn vero affirmationes, quod ad supradictam descriptionem revertentibus planius liquet; sensus ergo hic est. Ordo autem seriesque sermonum sese sic habel; ergo inquit Aristoteles contradictionem qua; est impossibile et non impossibile, illud quod est contingens et possibile, quæ dux affirmationes sunt ac sese sequuntur. et non contingens et non possibile, quæ duæ sunt negationes, sequuntur quidem contradictoriæ, ut contradictiones sint in contrarium ductæ, sed conversim, ut affirmatio negationem, negatio sequatur affirmalionem.
passages.english: But they follow conversely, because affirmation does not follow affirmation and negation negation; rather, negations follow affirmation and affirmations follow negation. This becomes plainer to those who go back to the diagram given above; this, then, is the sense. The order and sequence of the words is as follows. Aristotle says, then, that the contradiction "impossible" and "not impossible" follows "contingent" and "possible", which are two affirmations and follow one another, and "not contingent" and "not possible", which are two negations. The contradictories do follow, so that the contradictions are drawn in opposite directions, but conversely, so that affirmation follows negation and negation follows affirmation.
passages.notes: The construal of the long sentence is uncertain.
